newsitem.title: THAILAND: Bangkok Bank seeks Thai textile industry boost.
newsitem.headline: Bangkok Bank seeks Thai textile industry boost.

text.p: The Thai textile industry must address myriad structural problems to overcome its dwindling competitive advantage if it is to once again become a leading export earner, said a Bangkok Bank report on Monday.
Debunking suggestions that a reduction in Thai textile exports is cyclical the bank called for urgent solutions to restore the industry's competitiveness.
It said problems within the textile industry reflect similar problems faced by many Thai labour intensive industries.

"The problems which it (the textile industry) is currently facing are similar to those affecting other labour intensive industries of the country viz. footwear gems and jewellery. These problems are mostly structural in nature," said the report.
A decade of double digit export growth up to 1994 made Thailand the world's 13th largest textile exporter but the industry has faced a severe contraction recently.
Textile export growth declined by 12.4 percent in the first half of 1996 and is set to post negative growth this year.

The decline has been a significant contributor to a slump in Thailand's overall export performance which saw grew just 0.9 percent in the first nine months of this year, compared to 24 percent in the whole of 1995.

"The Thai textile industry has been developed to a level at which it is sizeable and quite sophisticated by even international standards. Its health has, therefore strong repercussions on the country's overall economy," said the report.

To reduce textile manufacturers' production costs in the short term the bank recommends cutting tariffs on petroleum imports which provide the raw materials for synthetic fibres and on capital equipment to increase factory automation and efficiency.
It recommended streamlining customs procedures to speed up tax refunds to exporters and offering cheap loans to smaller companies wanting to buy new machinery.
It suggested relocation of low-end manufacturing facilities to countries with cheaper labour pools, and a drive to open up new markets.

To ensure competitiveness in the long term it recommended the speedy establishment of a Textile Development Institute to promote exports and a shift in production and design to more upmarket products.
Direct sales into foreign markets would cut costs and increase margins while freer trade will help open up new export markets, said the report.

BBL's study is part of an ongoing drive by the Thai commercial banks to study Thailand's declining export industries and provide solutions to problems that have exaggerated the country's economic problems this year.
